en: The *Sūtra on Rāṣṭrapāla* Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling together with five hundred śramaṇas through the kingdom of Kuru, turning [the wheel of Dharma].
They arrived at the kingdom of Kuru-avarta.

The people of the country—the brahmins and the practitioners—heard that the Buddha had traveled and arrived in this land. Having heard of the Buddha’s wondrous and profound merits, they learned that he was free from greed, lust, anger, and delusion; that the words spoken by his heart were always upright and correct; and that having attained the Way of the Buddha, he knew of himself where he had come from in past lives and could foresee the events of the past, future, and present.
His eyes could see through all things, perceiving the destinies of birth and death and the paths of good and evil for all beings in the world, including those that crawl and wriggle.
In his walking he can fly and enter the earth; emerging from the unyielding and entering the solid without obstruction, he performs transformations with sovereign ease.
He knows the thoughts in the minds of the people of the world and all classes of crawling and wriggling creatures, knowing them all in advance.
The Buddha has self-mastery over his eyes, self-mastery over his ears, self-mastery over his nose, self-mastery over his mouth, self-mastery over his body, and self-mastery over his mind.
In the world there are ninety-six kinds of paths, none of which equal the Buddha-way;
the Buddha’s teaching of the people of heaven and earth is like parents instructing their children, enabling them to abandon evil and pursue good.
The Buddha acts as a teacher for the beings of the heavens above and the world below. Among the gods and people whom the Buddha instructs, all attain the path of Arhatship and Nirvana.
All the people within the kingdom say:
"The Buddha is an auspicious person who skillfully expounds the sutras and precepts; let us go together to behold his virtue and wisdom."

The people of that country—some in groups of fifty, some in groups of a hundred, and some in groups of five hundred—went together to where the Buddha was. Among them, some knelt before the Buddha; some circumambulated the Buddha three times; some placed their heads at the Buddha’s feet; some joined their palms; and some merely announced their surnames and names. Then all the people sat down.
The Buddha preached the sutras and precepts for the sake of the people, and all the people joined their palms toward the Buddha.
Among the assembly sat the son of an elder named Rāṣṭrapāla, who remained in his seat listening to the Buddha preach the sutra and taking it to heart.
Ratthapāla reflected to himself:
"One who follows the sūtras and precepts of the Buddha should not remain at home; those who live at home cannot purify themselves while training in the Way of the Buddha."
He thought to himself:
"It would be better for me to shave my hair, don the kashaya robes, and go forth as a śramaṇa.
When the people of the kingdom of Kauśāmbī heard the sutra and the precepts, they were all filled with joy; they circumambulated the Buddha three times and then each returned to their own homes.
Ratthapāla turned back midway and returned to where the Buddha was. He went forward, prostrated before the Buddha, joined his palms, knelt down, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I reflect that the sūtras and precepts of the Buddha are not suited for one living at home; those who live at home cannot purify themselves or study the Way of the Buddha’s sūtras."
"I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the *kāṣāya*, and become a śramaṇa.
I pray that the Buddha will have compassion for me and allow me to become a śramaṇa.
The Buddha said:
"Have you informed your parents? Ratahara replied,
"I have not yet informed my parents."
The Buddha said,
"It is the law of all Buddhas that one whose parents do not give permission may not become a śramaṇa,
nor may the precepts be conferred upon them. Rāṣṭrapāla said:
"I agree! Please return and inform my parents.
If my parents permit me to become a śramaṇa, I shall come back."
The Buddha said,
"Excellent! Reflect upon it yourself."
Ratthapāla then paid homage to the Buddha and returned to his parents, saying to them:

"According to what I have heard in the Buddha’s discourses and precepts, it is not appropriate to remain at home; those who live at home are unable to purify themselves while training in the path of the Buddha’s discourses."
"I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the *kāṣāya*, and become a śramaṇa.
When his parents heard their son's voice, they both wept facing one another and said:

"We, a husband and wife with but this one child, have prayed to the various heavens, the sun, and the moon, and prostrated ourselves on our foreheads toward the four quarters, seeking this child to continue our lineage. We have always feared that upon our deaths, our family line would perish."

"I obtained you, my only son, from heaven; the entire family holds you in deep affection and looks upon you without ever knowing satiety. Even if you were to pass away, we, husband and wife, would sit together by your corpse until our old age; how can you now wish to abandon us and depart?"
Ratthapāla said to his parents,
"If you do not now permit me to go to the Buddha's presence to become a śramaṇa, from this day forward I shall no longer drink, no longer eat, and no longer bathe."
"If you now permit me to become a śramaṇa, it will be well; otherwise, I shall face death!
He then lay prostrate on the bare ground and refused to eat for one day, two days, three days, four days, and reached the fifth day without food.

When the kinsmen and relatives of Rāṣṭrapāla, both near and far, heard that Rāṣṭrapāla had requested from his parents to become a śramaṇa and that his parents would not grant permission, they lay prostrate upon the bare ground, abstaining from all food and drink for five days.
The kinsmen and relatives from both within and outside the clan, totaling nine generations, all went to where Rāṣṭrapāla was. They spoke to him persuasively, urging him to rise, bathe, and eat.
They said to Rāṣṭrapāla:

"When your parents were yet without you, they offered prayers to the various heavens, the sun, and the moon, bowing their heads toward the four quarters to seek an heir; it was only with great difficulty that they obtained you, their one son."
"You ought to provide for your parents so as to continue the lineage of your family.
Even if you were to die, your parents would wish to sit and guard your corpse until they grow old; how much more so when you wish to depart from them while still alive?"
Ratthapāla did not respond.
His kinsmen and nine generations of relatives all went before his parents and wept, saying,
"This son will never accept our admonitions."

Ratthapāla had other close friends and acquaintances who, hearing that Ratthapāla intended to go to the Buddha’s presence to become a śramaṇa, and that his parents would not permit it, lay prostrate on the bare ground for five days, neither drinking nor eating.
His close friends and relatives all went to Rāṣṭrapāla’s place to exhort and persuade him to rise, bathe, and eat, saying to him:

"Before you were born, your parents offered prayers to the various devas, the sun, and the moon, prostrating themselves toward the four quarters in search of an offspring; it was only then that they obtained you, their only son."
"You ought to provide for your parents so as to continue the lineage of the family.
Even if you were to die, your parents would wish to remain by your corpse until they themselves grew old; how can you, on the contrary, wish to depart from them in life?"
Rāṣṭrapāla also did not respond.
His close friends and acquaintances then went before his parents, weeping and each wiping away their tears, and said to his parents:
"You should release this son and allow him to become a śramaṇa."
Why is this so? If those who delight in the Way become śramaṇas, they may later be born to meet one another;
but if they do not delight in the Way, they will naturally abandon the Way and return to the secular world.
"What else could be done?
Now you have been made to die in vain, rotting and putrefying to serve as food for worms and ants; what use is a corpse?
Now you are utterly disheartened and on the verge of death, while your parents, family, wife and children, female attendants, kinsmen, and friends all raise their voices in loud lamentation.

The parents wiped away their tears and said to Rāṣṭrapāla, "We have made a solemn agreement with our close kinsmen and friends: 'If you should go forth as a śramaṇa after we release you, will you then return to us so that we may see one another again?'"
Ratthapāla said: "Release me so that I may go to the Buddha and become a śramaṇa; this will ensure that I am born into a state free from death, and I shall certainly return to see my parents."
When his parents heard their son’s voice, they wept aloud once more, but they immediately granted him permission to go forth as a śramaṇa.
Ratthapāla was filled with great joy and thought to himself:
"I have not eaten for five days; my body is extremely emaciated."
At that time, the Buddha was traveling from the kingdom of Kauśāmbī to Śrāvastī, a distance of five hundred *li*.
He said, "I shall first attend to my own needs; I will set out only when I am strong and healthy."
Rāṣṭrapāla nursed himself for several days until he regained his strength, and then he went before his parents and said to them:
"Be at ease; I am going to the Buddha’s presence to become a śramaṇa."
The parents again raised their voices and wept bitterly;
wiping away their tears, they said, "You may go; take care of yourself.
Rāṣṭrapāla then placed his head at the feet of his parents, rose, circumambulated them three times, and departed.
He traveled to the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī, approached the Buddha, prostrated before him, and said:
"My parents have already granted me their permission; would the Buddha deign to accept me as a śramaṇa?"
The Buddha immediately ordained him as a śramaṇa; he donned the kāṣāya robe and received the śramaṇa’s sūtras and precepts.
The Buddha then instructed the arhats to teach him together every day.
Not daring to violate or injure the sutras and precepts, he contemplated the Way of the sutras and immediately attained the four dhyānas.

He then realized the first fruit of Srotāpanna, the second Sakṛdāgāmin, the third Anāgāmin, and the fourth Arhat. He further attained the four bases of supernatural power (*ṛddhipāda*) and the ability to fly; with the divine eye he perceived all things, and with the divine ear he heard everything. All beings above and below heaven, including those that crawl and wriggle, heard and knew his words and thoughts, and he himself knew his past lives and the origins from which he had come.
He followed the Buddha for ten years, like a shadow following a person.
After those ten years, he thought to himself:
"When I first left my home, I took leave of my parents, vowing that I would return to see them again."
Ratthapāla said to the Buddha:
"When I first left home, I made a vow that I would return to see you again; I wish now to go to where my parents are."
The Buddha thought of Rāṣṭrapāla, who was no longer able to enter into sensual desires as he had when he was a householder; he had already attained liberation from sensual desires.
The Buddha said: "Excellent!"
He immediately paid homage to the Buddha and departed.

Continuing his journey, he arrived at the kingdom of Kauśāmbī. Rising early in the morning, he donned his *kāṣāya* and took up his alms-bowl, entering the village where his parents lived to beg for food at their door.
No one in the entire household was willing to look at him. Why was this?
Because of the way of the śramaṇas, they had lost their master’s son; consequently, the whole family loathed seeing śramaṇas and would not look upon him.
When Rāṣṭrapāla arrived at his gate, there was no one to beg for alms, nor anyone to look upon him; no one addressed him, but only reviled him, yet he felt neither sorrow nor anxiety.
Just as he was about to leave home, a maidservant was about to go out with some foul-smelling bean soup dregs to discard them. Ratahara looked back and saw the servant, and asked her:
"What will you do with this foul-smelling bean soup?"
Then the maidservant said, "It is foul and unfit for further consumption;
that is why I wish to discard it. Ratahara replied:
"If you wish to discard it, sister, give it to me as alms.
The maidservant then placed it into his alms bowl.
The maidservant secretly recognized Rāṭṭhapāla by his hands, feet, voice, and manner of speaking, and she thought to herself:
"This is my master's son," she said,
and immediately ran inside to tell her mother,
"The master's son has arrived and is outside."

The mother was greatly delighted and said to her maidservant, "If it is truly as you say, then today I shall immediately grant you your freedom to become a commoner; I shall give you all the garments, coverlets, pearls, and rings currently upon my person."
The mother then ran to her husband’s location; at that time, the husband was in the middle courtyard combing his hair, and she said to him, "A maidservant saw my son Rāṣṭrapāla coming to this gate."
I said to my maidservant:

"If you have truly seen Rāṣṭrapāla, I shall strip off all the garments and jeweled bracelets from my body and give them to you as alms, and I will exempt you from servitude so that you may become a free citizen."
The mother said to her husband,
"Arise quickly and go out to search for him everywhere.
The husband immediately covered his head and ran through the streets, alleys, and lanes to search for him.
Seeing Rāṣṭrapāla in a secluded place looking up at the sun, having just received his meal, eating nothing but the dregs of stinking bean soup,
the elder spoke first to Rāṣṭrapāla:
"Should you not have come back home to sit comfortably and eat fine rice?"
"And yet you have instead stopped here to eat this stinking bean soup dregs?
Ratahara said to his father, "I have abandoned my home to study the Way as a śramaṇa; I have no home. How could I possibly obtain a home?"
The official called him to return home together, but he was unwilling to go.
The official then invited him for the following day, saying, "Come tomorrow; when you arrive at my house for a meal, you shall see your mother."
Ratthapāla said, "Very well!
He returned home and spoke to his mother-in-law, saying:
“Ratthapāla has indeed come here; I have already invited him for tomorrow’s meal.
Son, accept this invitation and prepare whatever is required in abundance.”
The mother immediately summoned all the male and female servants of the household to stand before her and said:

"When I first entered this gate, my parents gave me gold, silver, white pearls, and precious jewels; take them all out and place them upon the ground in the middle courtyard, covering them with objects."

The maidservant immediately followed her mistress's instructions and brought out all the gold, silver, white pearls, and precious jewels, piling them in the courtyard; the objects covered the ground, rising higher than a person’s head.
At mealtime, Rāṣṭrapāla donned his saṃghāṭī robe, took up his alms bowl, and went to his parents' house.

When his parents saw their son from afar entering the gate, the mother immediately took the piles of gold and silver that covered [the floor] and removed them, then stepped forward and scattered the gold and silver with both hands.
He said to Rāṣṭrapāla: "Behold this gold, silver, and precious jewels;

these were possessed by your mother when she entered the gate, and they were possessed by your father. There is immeasurable gold, silver, and precious jewelry; you may take it and use it for giving alms and food, and for your own great enjoyment."
"What is the use of being a śramaṇa?
It would be better to remain a white-robed householder.
Rāṣṭrapāla then spoke to his parents, saying:
"If you, Great Man, would follow my words, I wish to admonish you on one matter. His parents said, "Very well!"
"I shall obey your instructions," said Rāṣṭrapāla.

"Take the precious objects and use the covers to make bags; gather all the treasures and place them inside the bags. Load them onto carts and carry them to the banks of the Ganges, where you shall examine a deep spot and cast them therein."
Why is this so? Those who accumulate wealth and treasures cause themselves much anxiety; they may fear government officials or thieves, they may fear fire or water, or they may fear enemies.
The parents then thought to themselves:
"Ratthapāla cannot be converted by means of wealth and treasures.
Let us try to win him back by bringing back those beautiful women and female musicians from his former days."

The mother immediately went to where the beautiful women and handmaidens were, instructing them all to bathe and adorn themselves, putting on pearl bracelets and finery, and coming forth dressed in the garments that Raṭṭhapāla had previously enjoyed.
The mother instructed her beautiful concubines and handmaidens, saying:
"When you go out and see Rāṣṭrapāla, simply say: 'O son of a great householder!
What jade-like woman is superior to us that he would abandon us to go forth and study the Way, seeking yet another jade-like woman?'"
The beautiful women and maidens immediately followed their mother’s instructions, adorned themselves, and went out; the beautiful women and maidens then spoke to Ratahara, saying:
"Son of the Great Lady!"
"What jade maiden is there who excels us,
such that she would abandon us to go and study the Way,
seeking yet another jade maiden? Ratthapāla said:
"I did not abandon my sisters because I had no need for beautiful jade maidens.

When the beautiful ladies and court girls heard these words, they were immediately filled with shame and remorse; they knelt down on their long knees, bowed their heads, and covered their faces with their hands, saying:
"Since you will not take us as your wives, you instead call us 'sisters'!"
Ratthapāla said to his parents, "Why do you trouble me so?
If you wish to prepare a meal, that is well; if you cannot, then let it be."
The parents immediately set out food and utensils before him, and he began to eat.

The parents wished to watch their son for a long time, fearing that once he had finished eating he would leave; they therefore ordered all the doors to be closed and commanded that the door-keys be hung down.
When the meal was finished, he preached a sutra for his parents, saying:
"Wild people, domestic animals, and beasts should not be confined; when these animals cannot attain freedom, they abandon their keepers and flee."

"Once you have finished eating, you must depart. Having escaped, the wild beast fled into the deep mountains. Adorning the hair with combs, applying gloss, painting the eyebrows, using white powder and black collyrium—these things may indeed transform a fool; but they cannot transform one who has already seen the Truth. Why? Because such a person possesses the eye of wisdom. Just as a wise man would not take a poisoned bowl of rice, so too does one who has seen the Truth not accept these worldly adornments. Furthermore, if one were to apply these cosmetics to a corpse, it would only increase its loathsomeness. Therefore, one who has seen the Truth does not accept them. Moreover, these things are merely for the sake of vanity and pride, and they bring about the suffering of old age, sickness, and death. For this reason, one who has seen the Truth does not accept them. Furthermore, these things are like borrowed goods that must eventually be returned; they are like a dream from which one awakens; they are like a city of the Gandharvas that vanishes upon closer inspection; they are like a mirage that deceives the eyes; they are like a flame that flickers and goes out; they are like a bubble that bursts in an instant; they are like a dewdrop that dries in the morning sun; they are like a flash of lightning that appears and disappears; they are like a mountain stream that flows on without ceasing; they are like a jar of clay that will surely break; they are like a tree at the edge of a precipice that is liable to fall at any moment; they are like a house on fire that must be abandoned immediately; they are like a thief who must be driven away; they are like an enemy who must be subdued; they are like a snake whose head must be crushed; they are like a sword that must be sheathed; they are like a poison that must be expelled; they are like a disease that must be cured; they are like a debt that must be repaid; they are like a prison that must be escaped; they are like a wheel of fire that must be avoided; they are like a pit of coals that must not be entered; they are like a trap that must be shunned; they are like a net that must be torn apart; they are like a snare that must be cut; they are like a hook that must be pulled out; they are like a stake that must be removed; they are like a thorn that must be extracted; they are like a splinter that must be pried out; they are like a tumor that must be lanced; they are like a boil that must be drained; they are like a wound that must be bandaged; they are like a sore that must be treated; they are like a scab that must be healed; they are like a blister that must be popped; they are like a festering ulcer that must be cleansed; they are like a gangrene that must be amputated; they are like a tumor that must be excised; they are like a carbuncle that must be lanced; they are like a swelling that must be reduced; they are like a pain that must be relieved; they are like a fever that must be broken; they are like a delirium that must be cleared; they are like a stupor that must be dispelled; they are like a fainting spell that must be restored; they are like a paralysis that must be cured; they are like a convulsion that must be stilled; they are like a seizure that must be released; they are like a spasm that must be relaxed; they are like a cramp that must be loosened; they are like a contraction that must be expanded; they are like a stiffness that must be softened; they are like a rigidity that must be made supple; they are like a blockage that must be unobstructed; they are like a constriction that must be opened; they are like a knot that must be untied; they are like a tangle that must be disentangled; they are like a snarl that must be smoothed; they are like a wrinkle that must be ironed; they are like a fold that must be flattened; they are like a crease that must be pressed out; they are like a bulge that must be leveled; they are like a protrusion that must be smoothed over; they are like a hump that must be straightened; they are like a crookedness that must be made straight; they are like a curvature that must be made level; they are like a slope that must be made even; they are like a declivity that must be made flat; they are like a rise that must be made low; they are like a depression that must be raised; they are like a hollow that must be filled; they are like a gap that must be closed; they are like a breach that must be sealed; they are like a fissure that must be joined; they are like a rift that must be mended; they are like a crack that must be patched; they are like a hole that must be plugged; they are like a leak that must be stopped; they are like a drain that must be blocked; they are like a conduit that must be diverted; they are like a channel that must be dammed; they are like a torrent that must be diverted; they are like a flood that must be contained; they are like a surge that must be checked; they are like a gush that must be restrained; they are like a rush that must be slowed; they are like a flow that must be regulated; they are like a current that must be guided; they are like a stream that must be channeled; they are like a river that must be bridged; they are like a ford that must be made safe; they are like a crossing that must be prepared; they are like a passage that must be cleared; they are like a way that must be made passable; they are like a path that must be leveled; they are like a track that must be smoothed; they are like a trail that must be widened; they are like a route that must be made secure; they are like a road that must be maintained; they are like a highway that must be kept clear; they are like a thoroughfare that must be kept open; they are like a passage that must be kept free; they are like a gate that must be kept unlocked; they are like a door that must be kept ajar; they are like a portal that must be kept accessible; they are like an entrance that must be kept unbarred; they are like a threshold that must be kept clear; they are like a step that must be kept level; they are like a stair that must be kept firm; they are like a ladder that must be kept steady; they are like a bridge that must be kept sound; they are like a causeway that must be kept dry; they are like a dike that must be kept intact; they are like a wall that must be kept solid; they are like a rampart that must be kept high; they are like a fortification that must be kept strong; they are like a citadel that must be kept impregnable; they are like a stronghold that must be kept secure; they are like a bastion that must be kept watchful; they are like a tower that must be kept vigilant; they are like a lookout that must be kept alert; they are like a sentry that must be kept attentive; they are like a guard that must be kept ready; they are like a sentinel that must be kept on duty; they are like a watchman that must be kept awake; they are like a patrol that must be kept moving; they are like a guardhouse that must be kept manned; they are like a barracks that must be kept occupied; they are like a station that must be kept active; they are like a post that must be kept staffed; they are like a stationery that must be kept supplied; they are like a depot that must be kept stocked; they are like a storehouse that must be kept full; they are like a granary that must be kept filled; they are like a treasury that must be kept abundant; they are like a vault that must be kept rich; they are like a hoard that must be kept secure; they are like a reserve that must be kept intact; they are like a fund that must be kept available; they are like a capital that must be kept growing; they are like an investment that must be kept profitable; they are like a profit that must be kept increasing; they are like a gain that must be kept realized; they are like a benefit that must be kept enjoyed; they are like a reward that must be kept received; they are like a prize that must be kept won; they are like a victory that must be kept celebrated; they are like a triumph that must be kept proclaimed; they are like a glory that must be kept displayed; they are like a fame that must be kept spread; they are like a reputation that must be kept maintained; they are like a name that must be kept remembered; they are like a title that must be kept held; they are like a rank that must be kept attained; they are like a position that must be kept occupied; they are like a status that must be kept preserved; they are like a dignity that must be kept upheld; they are like an honor that must be kept respected; they are like a distinction that must be kept acknowledged; they are like a privilege that must be kept enjoyed; they are like a right that must be kept exercised; they are like a claim that must be kept asserted; they are like a demand that must be kept fulfilled; they are like an expectation that must be kept met; they are like a hope that must be kept
Those who have already transcended the world cannot be transformed by this.

To look upon the skeletal remains of a son, wrapped in skin and flesh, yet adorned with gold, pearls, earrings, pendants, and jade—approaching such people is like entering boiling water or fire; once in the fire, there is nothing left to cherish.
Incense and ointments may be used to transform the ignorant, but they cannot transform those who have transcended the world.

One who acts without self-awareness of what ought to be done cannot distinguish between father and mother, nor can one distinguish between elder and younger brothers; when the human heart harbors attachment, it cannot sever itself.

Women are like various bodies of water; as water flows into the great ocean, so do fools who turn toward women flow into the hells, among the animals, or among the hungry ghosts (preta). Those who wish to escape the sorrow and suffering of birth and death, and those who desire to attain the path of Nirvana, should keep themselves far removed from women.
Having finished preaching the sutra for his parents, Rāṣṭrapāla flew out through a skylight in the palace, escaping like a fierce lion that has broken free.
At that time, there was a king named Kṛkin, who had been close friends with Rāṣṭrapāla since their youth.
The king had a pavilion outside the city; Rāṭṭhapaṇḍita flew forward and entered the pavilion, where there was a tree named Vihāla, and he sat down beneath it.

At that time, King Kṛkin wished to go out to the hermitage for recreation and commanded the superintendent of the hermitage to prepare it for cleaning in advance. Upon receiving the command, the superintendent immediately went to clean it.
Seeing Rāṣṭrapāla sitting beneath the Veṇukāla tree in the hermitage, the superintendent saw him and went at once to inform the king:
"The cleaning is complete."
"Your Majesty may well speak of your close friend and acquaintance Ratahara; he is currently sitting under a tree in his hut.
Your Majesty may go to see him whenever you wish."
Upon hearing this, the king was greatly delighted and immediately prepared his carriage and set forth.
Arriving outside the hut, he alighted from his chariot and entered on foot to the presence of Rāṣṭrapāla; having paid his respects, he withdrew to sit down.
Ratthapāla said, "It is most excellent that the King has come! The King said:
"Although I have come here myself, you have been my friend since childhood; I wish to bestow wealth upon you to my heart's content.
Ratahara replied to the king, saying, "It is not fitting that you should bestow wealth upon me."
"Now that I have cast off my heavy burden and am released from prison, do you, O King, wish to place the burden of prison upon me once again?
It is not fitting that you should bring this to offer to me."
The king asked,
"With what kind of gift should I send you off? Rāṣṭrapāla replied:
“Your Majesty should simply say:

‘May my kingdom flourish, may the five grains ripen in abundance, and may the population be numerous so that alms are easily obtained; you may dwell within my realm, and I shall not allow my officials or subjects to oppress or wrong you.’”
The king said: "I accept your instruction; it shall be as you have wished, according to the words spoken by Ratahara.
Thus spoke the king.
"I wish to ask a question; I pray that you will listen to my words. Ratahāra replied, "Very well!"
The king then said:
"Ordinary people become śramaṇas because they undergo four kinds of suffering; it is for this reason that they practice as śramaṇas. What are these four?"
First is old age; second is illness and emaciation; third is solitude; and fourth is poverty.
It is only when a person possesses these four sufferings that they go forth to become a śramaṇa.
"Now, as I observe you, you clearly lack these four things; for what reason, then, have you become a śramaṇa?

The king said, "The reason one becomes a śramaṇa at an advanced age is that, as a person grows old, they reflect upon their own diminished strength and the difficulty of rising and sitting. They can no longer travel far to manage their livelihood or acquire wealth, and even if they possess property, they cannot maintain it firmly. For this reason, one shaves off the beard and hair and becomes a śramaṇa."

"As I observe you, there is absolutely nothing of this; your hair and beard are perfectly black and your body is complete. You are currently in the prime of life and should enjoy yourself. Your parents are weeping, for they do not wish for you to become a śramaṇa."

"Second, if a person is afflicted by a grave illness and their body has become emaciated, they think to themselves that they cannot earn a livelihood or acquire wealth, and even if they possess property, they cannot maintain it; for this reason, they shave their hair and beard and become śramaṇas.
I observe you, however, and see none of these conditions; you are not gravely ill, and your body is robust."

"Thirdly, there are those who are solitary and alone, unable to provide for their livelihood or acquire wealth; even if they possess property, they cannot maintain it, and for these reasons they become śramaṇas.
In me, however, I see none of this in you. With the exception of the royal kinsmen, I do not see anyone in my kingdom who surpasses you."

"Fourth, there are those who are impoverished, suffering from hunger and cold, with no means to provide for themselves; thinking to themselves that they are too poor to sustain a livelihood, they shave their hair and beards to become śramaṇas so that they may obtain alms to live by.
In my view, you possess none of these things at all. As I observe the wealthy people in the kingdom, none surpasses you."
"People become śramaṇas only because of these four sufferings.
The king asked:
"Are there not others besides these four matters who become śramaṇas?"

Ratthapāla said: “The Buddha constantly speaks of these four matters himself, having experienced them all; he uses them to instruct and admonish others. In my heart, I know for certain that it is as the Buddha has said; therefore, I have shaved off my beard and hair, donned the kāṣāya, and become a śramaṇa.”
What are the four? First, among those born into this world, there is none who can avoid aging; there is no one capable of halting the body so that it does not grow old.
Second, there is none who can avoid illness; there is no one whose body can take the place of another in death.
Third, when a person dies, they depart empty-handed, unable to carry away their wealth and property.
Fourth, until death, there is no one who can ever find satiety in sensual desires and material possessions; all people become slaves to their wealth and cravings.
"The Buddha has explained these four matters for me, and because my heart believes them, I have become a śramaṇa.
The king said, "You have explained these four matters too briefly; my mind does not understand them. I pray that you will explain them to me more extensively."
Ratthapāla said: "I shall ask the king himself; the king ought to answer me with sincerity.

When you were twenty, thirty, or forty years of age, in your physical strength, in archery and games, in mounting elephants and horses, and in your gait and speed—did you consider yourself at that time to have no equal?"

The king said, “It is truly as Rāṣṭrapāla says. When I was twenty, thirty, or forty years old, I considered myself peerless in archery, in riding elephants and horses, and in walking, trotting, and running.
Now that I am an old man, my strength has declined; it is difficult for me to sit or rise, and though I wish to leap over obstacles, I am unable to do so.”
Ratthapāla said, "The Buddha spoke of this one matter; for that reason, I shaved my hair and beard and became a śramaṇa.
The king said:
"The Buddha has spoken of these matters; they are truly marvelous and excellent, and have entered my heart.
Rāṣṭrapāla asked the king, "Are there not among the subjects any ministers or officials who depend upon the king for their livelihood?"
The king said, "Indeed, it is so. Ratahara replied:
“Has Your Majesty ever been afflicted by illness, weakened and confined to bed?
The King replied, “Indeed, there has.”
Ratthapāla said: "When I was afflicted by illness and confined to my bed, the King summoned his ministers and officials who depend upon him for their livelihood and commanded them, saying:
'Now that I am afflicted by this severe illness, you all must share in taking away my sickness.'"
"Even though the king were to give such an order, how could his ministers possibly share the king's illness and carry it away?
The king said, "No."
"One must experience this for oneself; a subordinate minister cannot take one's place.
Ratahara said, "The Buddha has spoken thus;
these are the two matters for which I have become a śramaṇa."
The king said, "Truly marvelous, truly excellent; it has entered my heart.
Ratahara asked the king:
"When a person's life comes to an end and they are about to die, it is something the human mind finds unpleasant; yet even though it is unpleasant, one cannot escape death."
Ratthapāla said, "If a person knows they are destined to die,
why do they not take precious jewels with them to the place where they are to be reborn?
The king asked:
"One cannot take precious jewels with one when being born into a future place; all must be abandoned, and one departs empty-handed.
Rāṣṭrapāla said, "The Buddha has spoken this;
these are the three matters for which I have become a śramaṇa."
The king said, “The Buddha’s teaching on this matter is truly marvelous and excellent; it has entered my heart.
Rāṣṭrapāla then asked the king:
"Does Your Majesty have peace and security within your realm, a flourishing population,
and an abundance of the five grains? The King replied, "I do."
Ratthapāla said: "If someone were to come from the east and speak the truth to the king, the king would surely believe what they say:
'I have come from the east; I saw a great kingdom there, where the land was fertile and the population was flourishing.'"
"I know the way and am able to lead the king's army to attack and seize that kingdom.
Upon hearing these words, would the king wish to send someone to go and seize that kingdom?
The king said, "Indeed;
though I covet its revenue, I still wish to take it. Ratahara said:
"Furthermore, if someone were to come from the south, the west, or the north, and report that there exists a kingdom such as the one in the east—would Your Majesty wish to take it?"
The king said, “Indeed,
though I covet its revenue, I still wish to take it. Rāṣṭrapāla said:
"Furthermore, suppose there were a person who came across from one side of the ocean and spoke to the king with utmost sincerity, and the king believed what he said:
'On the other side of the ocean there is a great kingdom, where the five grains flourish in abundance and the population is vast and prosperous.'"
"I know the way and am able to lead the king's army to attack that country.
Upon hearing these words, would the king wish to send someone to seize that country? The king said:
"Nevertheless, coveting its profit and revenue, one still desires to take it. Ratahara said:
"The Buddha, seeing this matter, knows that people suffer from greed and are never satisfied; these are the four matters for which I have become a śramaṇa."
"The Buddha sees these four matters and uses them to instruct and admonish people.
The king said, "The Buddha’s teaching on these matters is truly extraordinary and excellent; it has entered my heart."
The king said,
"Does the Buddha truly possess such excellence, knowing in advance the events of the past,
future, and present? Rāṣṭrapāla replied:
"The king possesses his own kingdom as well as those of the four quarters, yet he is never satisfied; he further covets the lands beyond the seas.

The Buddha observes that among the people of the world, those who possess wealth and treasures all hide them away securely, refusing to give anything to others; out of stinginess and greed they hoard them, while seeking more."

Both sovereigns and common people never know contentment; until death they do not abandon their craving for sensual desires. Yet they must inevitably leave this life behind, departing empty-handed with all their wealth and treasures. They shall proceed instead toward the realms of good or evil according to their own deeds.
Good and evil follow a person just as a shadow follows them.

After a person dies, their family and kinsmen weep and lament, enshrouding and burying them; yet in life a person is born alone, and in death they die alone. One’s body alone must bear the consequences of the good and evil one has committed; there is no one who can take one's place.
Consuming food, drink, gold, silver, and precious jewels cannot cause one to attain the Way; wealth and riches cannot rescue or protect a person's life from aging and death.
Human thoughts and concerns are manifold; what humans love and delight in causes their wills and intentions to shift repeatedly, preventing them from being single-minded.
The Buddha said:
"Because people indulge their own whims, they bring about calamitous changes, hostile encounters, and fear, just as a thief harbors such thoughts.

When others catch them from behind, they meet death through the evil they themselves have committed; likewise, when people of the world commit evil, after death they shall enter the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts."

It is like trees that produce flowers, leaves, and fruit: among them, some fall while they are still buds, some fall when they have become fruits, some fall when they are large, and some fall when they are ripe.
Human beings are also like this: some fall from the womb; some die upon hitting the ground; some die within half a year; and some die in old age. Thus, the lifespan of a human being is unknowable.
Ratthapāla said: "It is for this reason that I have become a śramaṇa; people say that because I am unable to manage a household, I have become a śramaṇa."
"Though there are various treatises and discourses, none are as essential as studying the Path.
When Rāḍha’s son had finished preaching this sutra, the king immediately attained the first stage of the *srotāpanna* and received the five precepts:
first, not to kill; second, not to steal; third, not to violate the wives of others; fourth, not to speak falsely or engage in double-tongued speech; and fifth, not to drink intoxicants.
Having received the precepts, the king prostrated and departed.
This concludes the *Ratthapala Sutta*, spoken by the Buddha.
